analysis.one_liner: Bars fossil fuel companies from federal COVID-19 business loans and freezes new federal oil, gas, and coal leasing.
analysis.headline: The bill to keep oil, gas, and coal companies out of federal COVID-19 bailout programs died in committee without a vote, with 43 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the CARES Act so companies that get 15% or more of their revenue from oil, gas, or coal could not receive federal pandemic loans or loan guarantees, and banks that take federal pandemic funds could not invest in those companies for two years. It would also freeze new federal oil and gas lease sales and coal leases, stop the Interior Department from cutting the royalties that drilling and mining companies pay taxpayers, and pause most new federal rulemaking until the COVID-19 emergency ends. The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would no longer underwrite loans to fossil fuel companies during the oil price crash, and would keep full royalty revenue from federal drilling and mining leases. Non-fossil-fuel businesses competing for limited federal relief funds, and communities affected by federal leasing, also benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Companies deriving 15% or more of revenue from oil, natural gas, or coal would be excluded from CARES Act loans, loan guarantees, and Defense Production Act financial assistance, reserving those programs for other businesses.

The Interior Secretary would be barred from reducing or eliminating royalties or net profit shares on federal leases, and existing statutory royalty-relief programs for onshore and deepwater production would be repealed, preserving revenue owed to taxpayers.
For the duration of the COVID-19 national emergency, Interior could not hold oil and gas lease sales, issue noncompetitive oil and gas leases, issue coal leases, or change fossil fuel regulations.

Banks receiving CARES Act funding (including money market guarantee users and community banks under the interim rule) could not take new ownership stakes in fossil fuel businesses for two years, and companies that took federal loans could not acquire new federal leases until repaying them.
Public comment periods open on March 13, 2020 would stay open past the end of the emergency, giving the public more time to weigh in on pending federal rules.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies lose access to federal pandemic credit, new federal leases, and royalty relief; their workers and lenders bear the knock-on risk during an oil price crash. Other federal agencies would have to pause most new rulemaking until 30 days after the emergency ends.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel companies, their lenders and workers

drawbacks.text: The bailout exclusion would have hit the oil and gas sector during the 2020 price collapse, and the sector's employees could have been among those hurt when their employers were cut off from federal credit.

The rulemaking freeze and extension of public comment periods apply to all federal agencies, not just fossil fuel regulators, which could delay rules unrelated to drilling, including rules needed to respond to the pandemic in other areas.

Cutting the Strategic Petroleum Reserve storage cap to 713.5 million barrels and barring privately owned oil from the reserve would reduce flexibility to store commercial crude during future oversupply.

The moratorium on lease sales and the two-year investment ban on banks are temporary emergency measures tied to the COVID-19 emergency declaration, not permanent policy, limiting their long-term effect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is real: during a pandemic-driven collapse in oil prices, the bill would have redirected limited federal relief money away from fossil fuel companies and preserved taxpayer royalties, but it would also have denied credit to a struggling industry whose employees did not choose the price crash, and its broad rulemaking freeze swept in agencies far beyond Interior. The relief-restriction and royalty provisions were targeted and low-cost; the agency-wide rulemaking suspension was the bluntest part of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four committees on the day it was introduced and sent to a Natural Resources subcommittee three weeks later, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 5, 2020, with 29 original cosponsors, and was referred to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Judiciary Committees the same day.
On May 27, 2020, the Natural Resources Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and no further action was ever taken.
All 43 cosponsors were House Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill never advanced out of committee or reached the House floor during the 116th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies were better off: they kept access to federal pandemic loan programs, new federal leases were never frozen, and the royalty-relief programs the bill would have repealed stayed in place. The banks that lend to them were spared the two-year investment restriction.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil, gas, and coal companies and their banks

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors such as Reps. Omar, Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, Pressley, Khanna, and McGovern.

sides.party_line_note: All 43 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republicans signing on, and the bill died without any recorded vote or recorded floor opposition.

industries.note: They would have lost access to federal pandemic loans and loan guarantees, faced a two-year moratorium on new federal lease sales, and lost statutory royalty relief. During the 2020 oil price crash, their interest in federal credit and cheap leases ran against the taxpayers who would have funded them.
They would have been excluded from CARES Act assistance and blocked from new federal coal leases and royalty relief for the duration of the emergency.

For two years they could not take new ownership stakes in fossil fuel businesses, cutting off a source of capital and fee income; their interest in that business ran against the public funds backing their balance sheets.

industries.industry: Federal lease operators (onshore and offshore royalty payers)
industries.note: The bill repeals royalty-relief authority and bars the Interior Secretary from cutting or eliminating royalties, so companies drilling on federal land and waters would have paid closer to full royalties to taxpayers.
